OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal



General OET Writing Tips and Tricks
  1. Understand the Task and Case Notes (Crucial 5 Minutes!):
      • Read the task first: Before anything else, read the writing task at the bottom of the case notes.
        This immediately tells you:
         • The type of letter (referral, discharge, transfer).
         • The recipient (who you are writing to).
         • The purpose of the letter (sometimes, it’s included in the case notes from the last visit).
         • This helps you identify the key information the reader needs to know.

        •   Read the first short paragraph (if present) at the top of the case notes: It lets you establish
            the context and confirm your role, specialty, and location.

        •   Allocate the first 5 minutes for reading:
             • Use this time to thoroughly read and understand the entire case notes.
             • Highlight or make mental notes of important information related to the patient's condition,
                history, current treatment, and future plans.

        •   Identify relevant vs. irrelevant information:
             • Not all information in the case notes needs to be included.
             • Filter out details that the recipient already knows or that are not directly relevant to their
               role in the patient's ongoing care. For example, if you're discharging a patient back to their
               GP, the GP likely knows the patient's basic demographics and long-standing conditions.
               Focus on new developments, current management, and discharge plans.

  2. Plan Your Letter (Structure is Key):
      • Outline:
           • Before writing, create a mental or quick written outline.
           • Decide what information to include and in what order.

        •   Standard Letter Format: Adhere to the formal letter format:
             • Recipient's Name and specialty: (e.g., Dr. [Name], [Specialty]).
             • Recipient's Address: (e.g., [Hospital/Clinic Name], [Address]).
             • Date: (e.g., 29 May 2025)
             • Salutation: (e.g., Dear Dr. [Name], or Dear Sir/Madam if name is unknown)
             • Reference Line: Re: [Patient's Full Name], [Date of Birth/Age] - Crucial for quick patient
               identification.

            •   Introduction Paragraph:
                 • Clearly state the purpose of the letter (e.g., I’m writing to refer…, etc.).
                 • Briefly introduce the patient (name and age).
                 • Clearly state the main presenting issue/reason for referral/discharge of the patient
                    (e.g., who was recently diagnosed with cancer colon, etc.).
                 • Clearly state what action you are requesting from the recipient (e.g., for your kind
                    assessment, etc.).




                                                                                                                1

            •   Body Paragraphs:
                 • Organize relevant information chronologically or by theme (e.g., medical history,
                   current presentation, investigations, treatment, progress, discharge plan). Inside each
                   paragraph, organize case notes logically.
                 • Use discourse markers (sometimes called "linking words" or "transition phrases")
                   appropriately.
                 • Group related information together in the same sentence, and use different sentence
                   types (simple, compound, and passive).
                 • Formulate case notes in your own words.
                 • Prioritize the most important information relevant to the purpose of the letter.
                 • Prioritize the most recent relevant information.
                 • Leave a blank line between paragraphs.
                 • Use indentation at the beginning of each paragraph.

            •   Conclusion/Request paragraph:
                 • Summarize the current situation.
                 • Clearly state what action you are requesting from the recipient (e.g., "I would be
                   grateful if you could take over Mr. Smith's ongoing care and monitor his blood
                   pressure." or "I would appreciate it if you could continue to review Ms. Jones's wound
                   and manage her pain as required.").
                 • Offer further information if needed (e.g., "Please do not hesitate to contact me if you
                   require any further information.").

            •   Closing: (e.g., Yours sincerely,)
            •   Your Title/Profession: (e.g., Nurse, Doctor, Physiotherapist etc.)

  3. Language and Tone:
      • Formal and Professional: Maintain a consistently formal and polite tone. Avoid slang,
        contractions (e.g., "don't," "can't"), and overly informal language.
      • Objective and Factual: Present facts and observations. Avoid personal judgments or emotional
        language.
      • Clear and Concise: Use clear, straightforward sentences. Avoid overly long or complex
        sentences. Get straight to the point.
      • Medical Terminology: Use appropriate medical terminology, but ensure it's understandable
        for the specific recipient. If writing to a non-medical professional (e.g., a community nurse in
        some contexts, or a social worker), explain complex terms briefly.
      • Accuracy: Ensure all medical facts, dates, medications, dosages, and patient details are
        accurate as per the case notes.
      • Grammar, Spelling, and Punctuation: These are crucial. Errors can affect clarity and your score.
        Proofread carefully.
      • Avoid "Suffers from": It's generally preferred to say "Mr. X has hypertension" instead of "Mr.
        X suffers from hypertension."

OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


   4. Conciseness and Clarity:
       • Word Count: Aim for the suggested word count (usually 180-200 words for the body of the
         letter, excluding address, date, salutation, etc.). While not a strict penalty for slightly exceeding,
         it encourages conciseness.
       • Combine Details and avoid redundancy:
          1. Reorganize the selected relevant case notes.
          2. Merge connected case notes into one sentence.
          3. Don't repeat information unnecessarily.

   5. Time Management:
       • You have 45 minutes for the writing sub-test.
       • 5 minutes: Reading and planning.
       • 30-35 minutes: Writing the letter.
       • 5 minutes: Proofreading and editing.

   6. Paragraphing: In the OET Writing sub-test, you have two choices for paragraphing. While both are
        technically acceptable, one is much safer and clearer for the examiner.

         A. Block Style (Highly Recommended)
            This is the modern standard for medical and business correspondence.
              • How to do it: Start every line flush against the left-hand margin.
              • Paragraph separation: Leave one empty line between paragraphs.
              • Why use it: It is the cleanest look and makes it very easy for the examiner to see your
                 structure at a glance.

         B. Indented Style
            This is an older, more traditional format.
              • How to do it: The first line of each paragraph is moved in by about 5–7 spaces. You do
                 not necessarily need to leave a blank line between paragraphs if you indent.
              • Why avoid it: It can look messy if your indentations aren't uniform, and it is easier to
                 accidentally miss a paragraph break.

Specific Tips for Referral Letters
    •   Purpose: To explain why the patient needs to be seen by another healthcare professional and what
        specific input is required.

    •   Introduction: Clearly state you are referring the patient, their name, age, and the primary reason
        for referral.

    •   Body:
         • Provide relevant medical history leading up to the current presentation.
         • Detail the patient's current symptoms, findings, and any investigations performed.
         • Explain any treatment initiated and the patient's response.
         • Include relevant social history if it impacts the referral




                                                                                                                  3
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


   •   Request: Be specific about what you are asking the recipient to do (e.g., "I would appreciate your
       urgent assessment regarding suitable pain management," or "I am referring Ms. Lee for a
       comprehensive neurological evaluation.").

   •   Referral Letter Opening Sentences: The key is to state clearly that you are referring the patient
       and the reason for the referral.
        • "I am writing to refer Mr. John Smith, a 67-year-old patient, for your urgent assessment
          regarding his worsening cardiac symptoms."
        • "Ms. Emily White, born on 12/03/1978, is being referred to you for further investigation and
          management of her persistent headaches."
        • "Thank you for seeing Mr. David Lee, a 45-year-old male, who presents with symptoms
          indicative of a possible deep vein thrombosis, requiring your urgent evaluation."
        • "I am referring Mrs. Sarah Green, aged 72, into your care for ongoing monitoring of her
          uncontrolled hypertension."
        • In conditions that don’t require referral, we use:
           a. I’m writing this letter to request/requesting your kind assessment of the workplace of Mr
              Jone, a 44-year-old patient of mine, who has clinical features suggestive of lumbar disc
              prolapse.
            b. I’m writing this letter in regard to/ regarding Mr Jone, a 44-year-old patient of mine, who
               has clinical features (or whose clinical features are) suggestive of/consistent with lumbar
               disc prolapse. Your assessment of his workplace would be highly appreciated.

   •   Referral Letter Finish Line:
        a. Simple Request for Assessment/Opinion
            • In view of the above, I believe that Mr John has features consistent with (or my provisional
              diagnosis is) lumbar disc prolapse.
            • "I would be grateful for your assessment and management of Mr. Henderson's persistent
              headaches."
            • "Your expert opinion on Ms. Davies' recurrent abdominal pain would be greatly
              appreciated."
            • "Thank you for seeing this patient and providing your recommendations regarding her
              ongoing care."
            • "I would appreciate your urgent review of Mrs. Chen's worsening cardiac symptoms."
            • "I would appreciate ordering a MRI scan for Mrs. Chen's and counseling her about the
              possibility of surgical intervention."

        b. Request for Specific Action/Intervention
            • "I would be grateful if you could assess Mr. Singh for potential surgical intervention for his
              fractured tibia."
            • "Please assess Mr. White for a comprehensive neurological evaluation and ongoing
              management."
            • "Your consideration of Ms. Tan for a gastric bypass procedure would be much appreciated."




                                                                                                               4
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


         c. Offering Further Information
             • "Please do not hesitate to contact me if you require any further information regarding Mr.
               Patel's condition."
             • "Should you require any additional details, please feel free to contact me."
             • "I am available to provide any further information that may assist your assessment."

    •   If there are multiple visits in the case notes:
         • When multiple visits occur, analyze the dates.
         • Close-proximity visits (within 1 - 2 weeks) usually relate to a single condition and subsequent
             visits usually describe response to treatment or review of test results; include all updates
             chronologically:
              • Combine the information into a single, flowing narrative paragraph. State the presenting
                  complaint and initial management. Use transition words to show progression and response
                  to treatment on subsequent visits.
             • Key Transitions: "Subsequently," "However, by [Date]," "Three weeks later, " "At the follow-
               up on [Date]," "Despite this," or "The condition then progressed to...". Avoid listing every
               piece of data from every single day unless it shows a critical change (e.g., vital signs
               worsening). Summarize the trend.
             • Example: "Ms. Smith presented on 1/11/2025 with severe abdominal pain. She was
               commenced on IV fluids. Despite this, her pain persisted, and a follow-up visit on
               3/11/2025 revealed a fever and elevated inflammatory markers, prompting admission for
               investigation."

         • Distant visits (e.g., years apart) mean earlier findings should be summarized under the
           patient's history, rather than described in detail:
            • The first paragraph after the introduction should focus on the most recent presentation,
               including the current problem and the reason for referral, as this is the examiner’s priority.
             • Place the findings from the older, distant visits into the patient history section of your letter,
               usually in a separate paragraph. This gives necessary background without cluttering the
               current narrative. When describing the present condition, only include the data from the
               most recent visit(s) related to the current referral reason.
             • Example: (In the History section) "Ms. Smith has a history of chronic kidney disease (CKD),
               first documented in 2018, managed with perindopril and regular monitoring." (Then in the
               body of the letter) "She is currently being referred for acute onset pyelonephritis..."

Specific Tips for Discharge Letters
    •   Purpose: To inform the ongoing care provider (usually, the GP or community nurse) about the
        patient's hospital stay, treatment received, current condition, and discharge plan.

    •   Introduction: State you are discharging the patient, their name, age, and the dates of admission
        and discharge, along with the primary diagnosis/reason for admission.




                                                                                                                    5
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


   •   Body:
        • Admission Details: Briefly state the reason for admission and initial findings.
        • Hospital Course: Summarize the patient's progress, investigations, and treatment provided
          during their stay. Highlight any significant events or complications.
        • Current Condition: Describe the patient's current medical status upon discharge.
        • Discharge Plan: This is crucial. Detail all follow-up appointments, new or ongoing medications
          (with dosage and frequency), wound care instructions, dietary advice, lifestyle modifications,
          and any referrals made.
        • Social/Support Needs: Mention any ongoing social support or community services arranged.
        • Request: Clearly state what ongoing care you expect the recipient to provide (e.g., "It would
          be appreciated if you could continue to monitor Mr. Brown's blood glucose levels and review
          his insulin regimen as appropriate," or "Please continue her regular medications as per the
          attached prescription and monitor her for any signs of infection.").

   •   Discharge Letter Opening Sentences: The key is to state that you are discharging the patient and
       briefly mention their admission/diagnosis.
        • "I am writing with regard to the discharge of your patient, Mr. Robert Brown, from St. Jude's
           Hospital today, following his admission for acute exacerbation of COPD."
        • "This letter is to inform you about the discharge of Ms. Olivia Davis, a 55-year-old female, who
           was admitted on [Date of Admission] with pneumonia and is now ready for transfer back into
           your care."
        • "Mr. Michael Johnson, born [DOB], who was admitted to our facility on [Date] following a
           fractured femur, is now being/ready to be discharged home and will require your ongoing
           community support."
        • "Thank you for accepting Ms. Sophia Miller, aged 30, back into your care following her recent
           appendicectomy at our hospital."

   •   Discharge Letter Closing Sentences:
        a. General Request for Ongoing Care
            • "I would be grateful if you could continue to manage Mr. Davies' medications and monitor
              his progress as outlined above."
            • "Your ongoing care of Ms. Chen would be greatly appreciated as she recovers at home."
            • "Thank you for resuming the ongoing care of your patient, Mr. Patel, following his
              hospitalization."
            • "Please continue to manage Ms. Lee's hypertension and monitor her for any
              complications."

        b. Emphasizing Specific Follow-up/Monitoring
            • "It would be appreciated if you could continue to monitor Mr. Brown's blood glucose levels
              and review his insulin regimen as appropriate."
            • "Please continue her regular medications as per the attached prescription and monitor her
              for any signs of wound infection."
            • "I would appreciate it if you could ensure Ms. Smith attends her follow-up physiotherapy
              appointments and address any concerns she may have regarding her mobility."
            • "Kindly monitor Mr. Johnson's neurological status closely and refer him for further
              assessment should his condition deteriorate."


                                                                                                             6
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


        c. Offering Further Information (Standard Professional Close)
            • "Please do not hesitate to contact me if you require any further information regarding Mrs.
              White's hospital stay or discharge plan."
            • "Should you have any queries regarding Mr. Henderson's care, please feel free to contact
              me."
            • "I am available to provide any additional details that may assist with Ms. Green's ongoing
              management."

   •   When Writing a Discharge Letter:
       1. Focus on the Hospital Course: Summarize the patient's stay, including the reason for
          admission, significant events, investigations performed, and treatment provided.

        2. Current Status on Discharge: Clearly describe the patient's current medical condition,
           including any residual symptoms, mobility status, and overall well-being.

        3. Comprehensive Discharge Plan: This is arguably the most critical section. Include:
            • Medications: New medications, changes to existing medications (dosage, frequency), and
              a clear rationale for changes. List all discharge medications.
            • Follow-up Appointments: Details of any scheduled appointments (specialist, GP, etc.).
            • Ongoing Care Instructions: Wound care, dietary advice, activity restrictions, symptom
              monitoring, and what to do if problems arise.
            • Referrals Made: Any new referrals to community services (e.g., physiotherapy, home
              nursing, social work).
            • Patient Education: What information has been provided to the patient and/or their family.

        4. Action Required from Recipient: Clearly state what you expect the GP or community nurse to
           do (e.g., monitor blood pressure, manage wound, continue medication, review symptoms).

        5. Clarity for Continuity of Care: The ultimate goal is to ensure a smooth transition of care and
           prevent readmission. The letter should provide all necessary information for the recipient to
           continue managing the patient effectively.

Specific Tips for an Update Letter
   •   Purpose: To inform the referring care provider (usually a GP or community nurse) about the
       patient's progress, the results of investigations, the definitive diagnosis, the treatment initiated,
       and the ongoing management plan since the patient was referred into your care.

   •   Introduction
        • Acknowledge the Referral: Thank the provider for referring the patient.
        • State Patient Details: Include the patient's name, age, and date of referral/initial
           consultation.
        • Restate Reason for Referral: Briefly mention the primary complaint or reason the patient was
           sent to you.
        • Purpose of the Letter: State that the letter is to provide an update on the patient's condition.




                                                                                                               7
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


        •   Example Opening Sentences:
             • "Thank you for referring Ms. Jane Doe, a 45-year-old female, to me on [Date] with a history
               of persistent headache. I am writing to update you on her diagnosis and management
               plan."
             • "I appreciate you entrusting Mr. David Chen to my care. He was referred on [Date] due to
               recurrent chest pain, and this letter outlines the findings from our recent investigations."
             • “I’m writing to update you on Ms. Garcia, a 30-year-old female patient who was referred
               by you into our care/department with suspected meningitis”

   •   Body
          1. Initial Assessment & Investigation Details
              • Initial Findings: Briefly summarize the key findings from your initial consultation (e.g.,
                  relevant examination findings, initial differential diagnosis).
              • Investigations: Detail the investigations that have been performed (e.g., blood tests,
                  imaging, specialized procedures) and their significant results.

            2. Definitive Diagnosis & Hospital Course (If Applicable)
                • Diagnosis: Clearly state the definitive diagnosis you have reached.
                • Hospital Course/Intervention: If the patient required a procedure, surgery, or a hospital
                   admission, briefly summarize the intervention and the patient's immediate post-
                   procedure progress (similar to a short hospital course summary).

            3. Treatment Initiated & Response
                • Treatment Plan: Clearly outline the treatment you have initiated (e.g., new
                   medications, lifestyle changes, physical therapy).
                • Patient Response: Describe how the patient has responded to the treatment so far,
                   noting any improvements or lack of response.

            4. Ongoing/Future Management Plan
                • Your Plan: Detail your ongoing plan for the patient (e.g., I will review her in 6 weeks,
                  We plan to schedule her for X procedure next month).
                • Referral to Other Specialists: Mention if you have referred the patient to any other
                  specialists and for what purpose.

            5. Request/Action Required from Recipient
                • Collaborative Care: Clearly state what ongoing care or monitoring you expect the
                  recipient to provide in the community while the patient remains under your specialist
                  care.

                •   Example Request Sentences:
                      • "It would be appreciated if you could monitor his blood pressure following the
                        recent medication change and adjust his current anti-hypertensive regimen as
                        appropriate."
                      • "Kindly continue to manage her Type 2 Diabetes and encourage compliance with
                        the recommended diet until her next appointment with me in three months."



                                                                                                              8
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


                     •    "Please monitor for any signs of wound infection and continue to provide analgesia
                          as required until she sees me for a follow-up review."

   •    Closing Sentences
          • Standard Professional Close: Offer to provide further information.
          • Example Closing Sentences:
             • "Please do not hesitate to contact me if you require any further information regarding Ms.
               Doe's ongoing care."
             • "Should you have any queries regarding Mr. Chen's management plan, please feel free to
               contact me."

   •    When Writing an Update Letter:
        1. Acknowledge and Validate: Start by thanking the referrer and restating the initial concern—
           this shows you understood the referral.
        2. Focus on the Update: Dedicate the main body to new information: investigation results,
           diagnosis, and treatment. This is the core reason for the letter.
        3. Be Specific with the Request: Your request to the referring provider is vital. It must be clear,
           actionable, and specific to ensure seamless shared care.
        4. Clarity for Continuity of Care: The ultimate goal is to keep the referring provider fully
           informed so they can effectively manage the patient's general health alongside your
           specialized treatment.

OET Assessment Criteria:
The OET Writing sub-test is assessed on six criteria:
    1. Purpose (0-3 points):
        • Is the purpose of the letter immediately apparent?
        • Is the purpose sufficiently expanded throughout the letter? (i.e., does the content support the
          stated purpose?)

    2. Content (0-7 points):
        • Is all relevant information from the case notes included?
        • Is irrelevant information excluded?
        • Is the information accurate as per the case notes?

    3. Conciseness & Clarity (0-7 points):
        • Is the letter free from unnecessary details?
        • Is the information presented in clear language?
        • Are sentences well-structured and easy to understand?

    4. Genre & Style (0-7 points):
        • Is the letter appropriate for the audience and purpose (formal, professional, objective)?
        • Is the tone appropriate?
        • Are conventions of letter writing followed?

    5. Organization & Layout (0-7 points):
        • Is the information logically organized into paragraphs?
        • Is the layout of the letter correct (address, date, salutation, etc.)?
        • Are linking words and phrases used effectively to ensure coherence?

    6. Language (0-7 points):
        • Accuracy of grammar, spelling, and punctuation.
        • Appropriate use of vocabulary, including medical terminology.
        • Range of grammatical structures.


Using Time phrases:
    1. To Refer to Past Events (Medical History, Admission, Initial Presentation): These phrases are often
       used with the past simple or present perfect tense.
        • On admission/Upon admission: Used to describe events or findings when the patient was first
           admitted to the hospital.
            • Example: "On admission, Mr. Jones presented with severe abdominal pain."
            • Example: "Upon admission, his vital signs were stable."

         •   Initially: Refers to the beginning of a period or condition.
              • Example: "Initially, Ms. Lee responded well to the intravenous antibiotics."
              • Example: "Her symptoms initially resolved with rest."




                                                                                                             10
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


        •   Previously/Prior to: Refers to events that happened before a specific point in time (e.g., before
            admission, before an operation).
             • Example: "Previously, Mr. Smith had no known allergies."
             • Example: "Prior to her surgery, Mrs. White experienced chronic knee pain."

        •   Subsequently: Refers to something that happened after something else.
             • Example: "He was subsequently diagnosed with Type 2 Diabetes."
             • Example: "Subsequently, his condition improved significantly."

        •   A week ago/Two days prior / Last [day/month]: Specific time markers for past events.
             • Example: "He reported a fall at home two days prior to admission."
             • Example: "Last Tuesday, she underwent a CT scan."

        •   In [month/year]/On [date]: For specific dates of past events.
             • Example: "In January 2024, she had a cholecystectomy."
             • Example: "On 15th May, he presented with a sudden onset of chest pain."

        •   Following [an event/procedure]: Used to describe what happened after a specific event or
            medical procedure.
             • Example: "Following the operation, he experienced some post-operative nausea."
             • Example: "Following his discharge, he will require daily wound dressings."

        •   Since then/Since [date]: To indicate a continuous period from a past point to the present.
             • Example: "He has been managing his diabetes well since then."
             • Example: "Since her admission on [date], her pain has significantly reduced."

        •   During hospitalization: Used to describe what happened after admission to hospital
             • Example: "During hospitalization, he experienced some nausea."
             • Example: " During hospitalization, he required daily assessment."

   2. To Refer to Ongoing/Current Events: These phrases often use the present continuous or present
      simple tense.
       • Currently: Refers to the present time.
          • Example: "Currently, Mr. Davies is mobilizing independently with a walking frame."
          • Example: "She is currently taking two medications daily."

        •   At present: Similar to currently.
             • Example: "At present, the patient's blood pressure is stable."

        •   Ongoing: To describe something that is continuing.
             • Example: "She requires ongoing physiotherapy."
             • Example: "His pain management is ongoing."

        •   Since [date of admission/beginning of treatment]: If referring to a condition or progress that
            started in the past and continues to the present.
             • Example: "Since her admission, Ms. Chen's fever has subsided."



                                                                                                                11
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


    3. To Refer to Future Events (Discharge Plan, Follow-up): These phrases often use future tenses (will,
       is/are to be, scheduled for, planned for).
        • Upon discharge / On discharge: To describe what will happen immediately after discharge.
            • Example: "Upon discharge, Mr. Patel will require supervision with his medication."
            • Example: "On discharge, his regular medications will be continued."

         •   Following discharge: Similar to "upon discharge," but can refer to events occurring after the
             immediate discharge.
              • Example: "Following discharge, Mrs. Davies will have a follow-up appointment in one
                 week."

         •   In [number] days/weeks/months: For future timeframes.
              • Example: "He is scheduled for a review in two weeks."
              • Example: "His staples are to be removed in 10 days."

         •   As of [date]: Used to indicate a change or new status from a specific date.
              • Example: "As of tomorrow, he will begin a new rehabilitation program."

        Example of combining phrases in a paragraph:
               "Mr. Thompson, a 68-year-old male, was admitted on 20th May with acute chest pain.
          Initially, he was managed with analgesia and oxygen. Subsequently, a coronary angiogram was
          performed, which revealed significant stenosis. Currently, he is stable and pain-free. Following
          his discharge today, he will require close monitoring and a review appointment in two weeks."

Using articles:
    1. Indefinite Articles: 'A' and 'An': These are used when you are referring to a singular, countable
       noun for the first time, or when you are talking about something in a general sense, not a specific
       one.
        • Mr. Jones presented with a persistent cough.
        • She reported a throbbing headache that began this morning.
        • Mrs. Chen developed a low-grade fever last night.
        • On examination, there was a pruritic rash on her chest.
        • He is suffering from a severe sore throat.
        • The patient requires a surgical consultation regarding his knee.
        • He is a smoker.
        • He has a history of hypertension. (Note: The phrase 'a history of' is countable, even though
          the disease 'hypertension' itself is not.)
        • She reported an ache in her left knee.
        • She reported pain in her left knee.
        • He sustained an acute injury to his ankle.
        • He underwent an emergency procedure this morning.
        • He has an uncontrolled blood pressure despite medication.
        • An MRI scan was performed.




                                                                                                             12
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


    2. Definite Article: 'The' 'The' is used when you are referring to a specific noun that is already known
       to the reader, or is unique, or has been previously mentioned.

    3. Zero Article (No Article) There are many instances in medical writing where no article is used.
        • Plural Countable Nouns (general sense):
           • Example: "Patients often require antibiotics for bacterial infections." (general antibiotics,
              not specific ones)
           • "He responded well to painkillers."
           • "She has several allergies."

         •   Uncountable Nouns (general sense): Many medical terms are uncountable.
              • Example: "He received treatment for pneumonia."
              • "She was given fluid intravenously."
              • "He has diabetes."
              • "She requires physiotherapy."
              • "He is on hypertension medication." (Referring to the condition itself, not a specific type)

         •   Names of specific diseases/conditions (most common): Many major diseases, especially
             chronic ones, do not take an article.
              • Example: "He suffers from hypertension." (versus a history of hypertension)
              • "She was diagnosed with diabetes."
              • "He has a history of asthma."
              • "She has cancer."

         •   Activities/Concepts (general):
              • Example: "He requires surgery." (versus a surgical intervention)
              • "She needs rest."
              • "He tolerates food well."

         •   With 'by' + means of transport:
             • Example: "He travelled by ambulance."

Abbreviations: The choice between 'a' and 'an' for abbreviations (like MRI, X-ray, ICU) depends on the
sound of the first letter, not the letter itself.
   • An MRI (sounds like 'em')
   • An X-ray (sounds like 'ex')
   • A CT scan (sounds like 'see')
   • Check the case notes: Often, the case notes will hint at article usage. If it says "recurrent chest
       pain," you might write "a history of recurrent chest pain" or "he presented with recurrent chest
       pain." If it says "fractured tibia," it's "a fractured tibia."

Examples with common terms:
  Talking about History:
    • “The patient has a history of…”
    • “There is a known history of…”
    • “The patient’s medical history includes…”



                                                                                                               13
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


   •   "He is a smoker." (characteristic)
   •   "He is a drinker/a social drinker. He drinks socially".
   •   "He is a heavy smoker."
   •   "He has a history of being a smoker."
   •   "She quit smoking shorty after her childbirth. "
   •   "She has a history of hypertension."
   •   "There is a known family history of depression."
   •   "He was diagnosed with essential hypertension."
   •   "She has hypertension."
   •   "She is hypertensive/diabetic. "
   •   “Please note that he/she is allergic to ..”

 Describing Symptoms:
  • “The patient reports experiencing…”
  • “There is evidence of…”
  • “The patient presents with…”
  • “The patient complains of…”
  • “Symptoms include…”

 Describing Examination Results:
  • “His examination was unremarkable, except for …”
  • “Examination revealed/showed …”

 Ordering Investigations:
  • “I recommend an MRI/CT scan to further evaluate…”
  • “Please arrange for blood tests to assess…”
  • “An ultrasound is advised to investigate…”
  • “I would like to order an MRI to…”
  • “An urgent CT scan is warranted to…”
  • “Please consider an ultrasound for further assessment.”
  • "I would like to request an MRI scan for the patient to evaluate the underlying condition. "
  • "Could you please arrange a CT scan to get a better view of the area in question? "
  • "I recommend scheduling an MRI scan to further investigate the symptoms. "

 Receiving Investigation Results:
  • “The results of the MRI indicate…”
  • “The CT scan revealed…”
  • “Laboratory results show…”
  • “One week later the patient came back for the test results, which revealed …”
  • “Test results revealed/showed …”

 Treatment plan of action:
   • "He is scheduled for surgery next week."
   • "He recovered well from the gastric bypass surgery."
   • "He requires surgery to repair the fracture."
   • “We will initiate treatment with…”



                                                                                                   14
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


   •   “Begin/commence/start the patient on…”
   •   “Administer… as the first line of treatment.”
   •   “Surgery is recommended to…”
   •   “A surgical intervention is necessary for…”
   •   “The patient will require surgery to…”
   •   “Please schedule the surgery for…”
   •   “Arrange for the patient to undergo surgery on…”
   •   “Implement a plan that includes…”
   •   “Monitor the patient’s response to…”
   •   “Adjust the dosage of… as needed.”
   •   “Provide supportive care alongside…”
   •   “Recommend a balanced diet rich in…”
   •   “Advise the patient to reduce/on reducing … and increase/increasing …”
   •   “Incorporate more fruits and vegetables into the diet.”
   •   “Limit the intake of…”
   •   “Encourage the patient to maintain a healthy lifestyle by…”
   •   “Advise stress-reducing activities such as…”
   •   “Advise the patient to avoid smoking and limit alcohol consumption.”
   •   “Recommend regular physical activity, such as…”
   •   “Advise the patient to engage in at least 30 minutes of exercise daily.”
   •   “Encourage activities that promote cardiovascular health, like walking or cycling.”
   •   “Incorporate strength training exercises twice a week.”

Discourse Markers in Professional Writing:
   1. Addition and Emphasis (To add related information or detail)
       • The patient's blood pressure remains elevated. In addition, his recent lipid panel showed
         hypercholesterolemia.
       • The wound shows signs of local infection. Furthermore, the patient's temperature has
         increased from 37.5°C to 38.9°C.
       • The initial blood tests confirmed an electrolyte imbalance. Moreover, the renal function
         markers showed acute deterioration.
       • The family reports previous episodes of unexplained syncope. Additionally, the patient has a
         known allergy to Penicillin.

   2. Contrast and Concession (To show difference, contradiction, or unexpected results)
       • The patient's pain score decreased initially with Tramadol. However, he now reports
         breakthrough pain every four hours.
       • The imaging study was inconclusive regarding the primary diagnosis. Nevertheless, given the
         clinical presentation, we initiated empirical antibiotic therapy.
       • Surgical intervention carries a risk of nerve damage. On the other hand, delaying the
         procedure may lead to permanent loss of mobility.
       • His inflammatory markers were highly elevated on admission. In contrast, the latest lab work
         shows a significant reduction in CRP levels.
       • The patient continues to experience frequent nocturnal leg cramps. Despite this, she denies
         any major impact on her overall sleep quality.



                                                                                                        15
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


    3. Cause and Effect (To explain reasons or logical results)
        • The biopsy confirmed a malignancy of the lung. Therefore, I am referring the patient to the
          oncology department for further management.
        • The medication caused severe gastrointestinal distress. Consequently, the dosage was
          reduced by half, and a PPI was prescribed.
        • His fluid input has significantly outpaced his output over the last 48 hours. As a result, we will
          discontinue IV fluids and commence a diuretic.
        • We have managed the acute respiratory distress and stabilized his vital signs. Thus, he is now
          medically fit for transfer back to the general ward.
        • Due to the patient's history of atrial fibrillation, we must proceed cautiously with general
          anesthesia.

    4. Summarizing and Conclusion (To wrap up a point or the entire discussion)
        • In summary, Mr. Jones's condition is complex, requiring a multidisciplinary approach focusing
          on pain control and physical rehabilitation.
        • Overall, her response to the new antihypertensive regimen has been positive, with blood
          pressure consistently below 140/90 mmHg.
        • To conclude, I believe this patient requires urgent review by a consultant cardiologist to
          investigate the recurrent atypical chest pain.
        • The patient's recovery has been excellent, requiring minimal analgesic support. In short, she
          is now ready for discharge.

    5. Sequencing and Order (To structure a process or argument)
        • Firstly, I request a complete blood count. Secondly, an abdominal ultrasound would be
          beneficial to assess the liver.
        • The patient was monitored in the Emergency Department for six hours. Subsequently, his
          symptoms completely resolved, and he was discharged.
        • We have addressed the infection and corrected the nutritional deficits. Finally, a follow-up
          appointment has been scheduled for two weeks.

Identifying relevant vs irrelevant notes:
The Golden Rule: The Recipient and the Purpose
Always ask yourself these two questions:
  1. Who is the recipient? (e.g., GP, specialist, community nurse, physiotherapist, social worker). Will
     this case note affects how the recipient will continue care for the referred patient? or does the
     recipient need to know this case note to properly continue care for the referred patient?
 2. What is the purpose of the letter? (e.g., referral for specialist opinion, discharge for ongoing care,
    transfer to another facility, advice to a community service). Is this case note relevant to the purpose
    of the letter?

      The answers to these questions will dictate what information is relevant. Information is relevant if
the recipient needs it to effectively carry out their role in the patient's ongoing care based on the stated
purpose.




                                                                                                               16
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


Factors to Consider for Relevance:
1. Existing Relationship with the Patient:
     • If the recipient already knows the patient (e.g., GP for a discharge letter):
         • Less relevant: Long-standing past medical history (unless it directly impacts the current
            admission/discharge), basic social history (marital status, occupation, number of children) they
            likely already have on file.
         • Relevant: New diagnoses, changes in existing conditions, details of the recent hospital stay,
            new medications, changes to old medications, specific discharge instructions, new referrals,
            any recent significant social changes (e.g., loss of a spouse, new care arrangements).

    •   If the recipient does NOT know the patient (e.g., specialist for a referral letter):
         • More relevant: Concise but comprehensive relevant past medical history, relevant social
             history (e.g., if social circumstances impact their condition or adherence to treatment), current
             living situation. They need a broader picture to understand the patient.
         • Less relevant: Highly detailed social history (e.g., hobbies, specific financial details) unless it
             directly impacts the patient's condition or the reason for referral.

2. Recipient's Role/Specialty:
    • What does this particular professional need to know to do their job?
    • To a Cardiologist (referral for chest pain):
         • Relevant: history of cardiac issues, risk factors (smoking, hypertension, diabetes), nature of
           chest pain, results of ECGs, troponins, stress tests, medications for cardiac conditions, family
           history of heart disease.
         • Irrelevant: detailed history of a childhood ear infection, a minor ankle sprain from years ago
           (unless related to mobility for cardiac rehab).

   •    To a Physiotherapist (referral for mobility issues):
         • Relevant: mechanism of injury, type of fracture, surgical procedure details, weight-bearing
            status, current mobility level, pain assessment, home environment, need for aids, patient's
            goals.
         • Irrelevant: detailed blood test results not related to physical function, specific antibiotic
            regimen.

   •    To a GP (discharge post-surgery):
         • Relevant: surgical procedure, complications, post-op instructions, wound care, new
            medications, follow-up appointments, general condition on discharge, advice given to patient.
         • Irrelevant: minute-by-minute details of the operation, nurse's detailed shift notes on general
            observations unless they reflect a significant change or complication.

3. Purpose of the Letter:
    • Referral Letter: Focus on why the patient needs to be seen by this specialist.
        • Relevant: Presenting complaint, history of presenting complaint, relevant past medical history,
          previous treatments for this complaint and their effectiveness, relevant social history
          influencing the complaint or management, any investigations performed, the specific question
          or request you have for the specialist.



                                                                                                                 17
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


         •   Irrelevant: Information unrelated to the chief complaint or the reason for referral, excessive
             detail about minor past illnesses, family history not related to the current issue.

   •    Discharge Letter: Focus on the hospital stay and the plan for ongoing care.
         • Relevant: Reason for admission, brief summary of hospital course (key investigations,
            diagnoses, treatments, progress), patient's condition on discharge, new/changed medications
            (dose, frequency, route), specific discharge instructions (wound care, diet, activity), follow-up
            appointments, new referrals, social/community support arranged.
         • Irrelevant: Daily routine notes unless they indicate a significant trend or event, very minor or
            resolved symptoms that don't impact discharge, routine lab results unless they represent a
            critical change or new diagnosis.

4. Chronology and Urgency:
    • New vs. Old Information: New developments, recent changes, and current status are generally
       more relevant than very old, stable conditions unless they directly impact the current situation.
    • Urgency: If the case notes indicate an urgent referral, prioritize information that highlights the
       urgency and potential risks if not addressed promptly.

5. Conciseness and Clarity:
    • Avoid Redundancy: Don't repeat information if it's already been stated clearly.
    • Summarize: Instead of listing every single symptom, summarize them (e.g., "Mr. X presented with
       classical symptoms of appendicitis," rather than listing every stomach pain detail).
    • Filter Minor Details: If the patient had a temporary, easily resolved issue during hospitalization
       that doesn't impact their discharge or ongoing care, it might be irrelevant to include.

Practical Steps During the 5-Minute Reading Time:
   1. Read the Writing Task First: This immediately gives you the recipient and purpose.
   2. Skim the Entire Case Notes: Get a general overview of the patient's story.
   3. Go Through Each Note Systematically:
         • For each piece of information, ask: "Does [Recipient] need to know this to do [Purpose]?"
         • Highlight or circle key relevant information.
         • Mentally (or lightly, if allowed) cross out clearly irrelevant information.
         • Categorize relevant notes into logical paragraphs (e.g., presenting complaint, medical history,
            investigations, treatment, discharge plan).

   4. Prioritize: Within relevant notes, decide what is most important and what can be summarized.

OET Writing noun-verb Collocations List
    1. Presenting Complaints & History
         • To present with + symptom
           Example: The patient presented with acute chest pain.
         • To complain of + symptom
           Example: She complained of persistent dizziness.
         • To report + symptom/change
           Example: The patient reported worsening shortness of breath.



                                                                                                                18
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


        • To deny + symptom/history
          Example: She denied fever or recent trauma.
        • To have a history of smoking / hypertension
          Example: He has a history of smoking and hypertension.

   2. Injuries & Conditions
        • To sustain an injury
          Example: He sustained a wrist injury following a fall.
        • To suffer from diabetes / asthma
          Example: She suffers from type 2 diabetes.
        • To develop complications / symptoms
          Example: The patient developed post-operative complications.
        • To contract an infection
          Example: He contracted a urinary tract infection.
        • To experience pain / dizziness
          Example: She experienced severe abdominal pain.

   3. Diagnosis
        • To be diagnosed with + condition
          Example: She was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes.
        • To confirm a diagnosis
          Example: Blood tests confirmed the diagnosis.
        • To rule out + condition
          Example: Imaging was performed to rule out malignancy.

   4. Investigations & Tests
        • To conduct a test
          Example: A blood test was conducted on admission.
        • To perform an examination
          Example: A physical examination was performed.
        • To order blood tests
          Example: Routine blood tests were ordered.
        • To undergo investigations
          Example: She underwent further investigations.
        • To request imaging (X-ray / CT / MRI)
          Example: A chest X-ray was requested.
        • To review test results
          Example: The results were reviewed the following day.
        • To monitor vital signs
          Example: Vital signs were closely monitored.
        • To be unremarkable
          Example: Physical examination was unremarkable, except for mild leg swelling.
        • To be normal
          Example: Cardiovascular examination was normal.
        • To be within normal limits
          Example: Vital signs were within normal limits.
        • To remain within normal limits
          Example: Blood glucose levels remained within normal limits.



                                                                                          19
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


        • To reveal no abnormalities
          Example: Neurological examination revealed no abnormalities.
        • To show no significant findings
          Example: Imaging showed no significant findings.
        • To be stable
          Example: The patient’s observations were stable.
        • No evidence of + condition
          Example: There was no evidence of infection.
        • No signs of + condition
          Example: There were no signs of heart failure.

   5. Treatment & Management
        • To undergo surgery
          Example: The patient underwent surgery without complications.
        • To commence treatment
          Example: Treatment was commenced immediately.
        • To initiate therapy
          Example: Physiotherapy was initiated post-operatively.
        • To start on medication
          Example: She was started on oral antibiotics.
        • To administer a drug
          Example: Intravenous antibiotics were administered.
        • To prescribe medication
          Example: Paracetamol was prescribed for pain relief.
        • To adjust the dosage
          Example: The dosage was adjusted accordingly.
        • To discontinue treatment
          Example: The medication was discontinued due to side effects.
        • To respond well to treatment
          Example: The patient responded well to treatment.
        • To be advised on (plan, options, steps, management)
          Example: The patient was advised on further investigations/starting management.
          Example: He was advised on exercise and diet plans.
        • To be advised to (what to do, i.e., a recommendation)
          Example: The patient was advised to start treatment.
          Example: The patient was advised to exercise.
        • To be advised about (information, risks, need, condition, explanation, awareness)
          Example: The patient was advised about the need for a synovial fluid sample/the risks of surgery.
          Example: The patient was advised about the possible risks of surgery.

   6. Hospital Care
        • To be admitted to hospital
          Example: He was admitted to hospital for further management.
        • To remain under observation
          Example: She remained under observation overnight.
        • To be discharged home
          Example: The patient was discharged home yesterday.
        • To attend follow-up
          Example: He was advised to attend follow-up in two weeks.


                                                                                                              20
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


        • To require further management
          Example: She requires further management by your team.
        • To be referred to a specialist
          Example: The patient was referred to a cardiology specialist.

   7. Progress & Outcome
        • To show gradual improvement
          Example: The patient showed gradual clinical improvement.
        • To remain stable
          Example: His condition remained stable throughout admission.
        • To deteriorate
          Example: The patient’s condition deteriorated overnight.
        • To make a full recovery
          Example: She is expected to make a full recovery.
        • To have an uneventful recovery
          Example: He had an uneventful post-operative recovery.




                                                                          21
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal



Example discharge letter structure:

Dr Stevens
Mill Street Surgery
Farnham
GU10 1HA

20/12/2025

Dear Dr Stevens,
RE: Mrs Sally Fletcher, DOB: 3/10/1993

I’m writing with regard to Mrs Fletcher, a 32-year-old married accountant, who has recently undergone a
laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis and now is ready to be discharged back into your care.

Upon admission, Mrs Fletcher underwent a transvaginal ultrasonography, which revealed a 6-cm cyst,
likely of endometrial origin. Therefore, laparoscopic surgery was scheduled and was uneventful. Today,
she is being discharged after she was made sure to be able to eat, ambulate and urinate independently.
Please make sure the wound is kept clean and dry.

Regarding postoperative mobility, she may shower from tomorrow and should avoid driving when on
analgesics. Additionally, she can resume her sexual life in 2 weeks. At home, she may return back to her
normal diet and ambulate as tolerated, and should be encouraged to drink oral fluids. Please note that
upon discharge, all her laboratory tests were within normal ranges. Moreover, she was alert, oriented and
comfortable. I also made sure someone will drive her home.

Your ongoing care for Mrs Fletcher after discharge and regular follow up visits would be highly
appreciated. Should you need any further information, please contact me.

Yours sincerely,
Doctor




                                                                                                            22
 
OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal



Example referral letter structure:

Dr Dev Desai
Gastroenterologist
City Hospital
Easton

30/8/2019

Dear Dr Desai,
RE: Mr Adam Knowles, DOB: 22/8/1951

Thank you for urgently seeing Mr Knowles, a 68-year-old retired management consultant, whose features
are suggestive of pancreatic malignancy. Your urgent assessment and possible endoscopy would be highly
appreciated.

Mr Knowles, who is a non-smoker, but a social drinker, first presented a month ago with heartburn, for
which OTC antacids were not effective. Full clinical examination was unremarkable. Therefore, FBC and
LFT were ordered. Moreover, he was started on Omeprazole 20mg twice daily.

On today's visit, he came back to review the test results, which showed high bilirubin, amylase, ALT,
albumin and alkaline phosphatase levels. Additionally, the patient reported a recent onset of diarrhoea,
pale stools, abdominal pain and fatigue. Examination also revealed a tender, swollen abdomen and a 2-kg
weight loss since the last visit. Jaundice was noticed as well.

In view of the above, my provisional diagnosis is pancreatic malignancy. Therefore, your urgent
assessment and possible endoscopy would be highly appreciated. Should you need any further
information, please contact me.

Yours sincerely,
Doctor




                                                                                                           23

OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal



General OET Writing Tips and Tricks
  1. Understand the Task and Case Notes (Crucial 5 Minutes!):
      • Read the task first: Before anything else, read the writing task at the bottom of the case notes.
        This immediately tells you:
         • The type of letter (referral, discharge, transfer).
         • The recipient (who you are writing to).
         • The purpose of the letter (sometimes, it’s included in the case notes from the last visit).
         • This helps you identify the key information the reader needs to know.

        •   Read the first short paragraph (if present) at the top of the case notes: It lets you establish
            the context and confirm your role, specialty, and location.

        •   Allocate the first 5 minutes for reading:
             • Use this time to thoroughly read and understand the entire case notes.
             • Highlight or make mental notes of important information related to the patient's condition,
                history, current treatment, and future plans.

        •   Identify relevant vs. irrelevant information:
             • Not all information in the case notes needs to be included.
             • Filter out details that the recipient already knows or that are not directly relevant to their
               role in the patient's ongoing care. For example, if you're discharging a patient back to their
               GP, the GP likely knows the patient's basic demographics and long-standing conditions.
               Focus on new developments, current management, and discharge plans.

  2. Plan Your Letter (Structure is Key):
      • Outline:
           • Before writing, create a mental or quick written outline.
           • Decide what information to include and in what order.

        •   Standard Letter Format: Adhere to the formal letter format:
             • Recipient's Name and specialty: (e.g., Dr. [Name], [Specialty]).
             • Recipient's Address: (e.g., [Hospital/Clinic Name], [Address]).
             • Date: (e.g., 29 May 2025)
             • Salutation: (e.g., Dear Dr. [Name], or Dear Sir/Madam if name is unknown)
             • Reference Line: Re: [Patient's Full Name], [Date of Birth/Age] - Crucial for quick patient
               identification.

            •   Introduction Paragraph:
                 • Clearly state the purpose of the letter (e.g., I’m writing to refer…, etc.).
                 • Briefly introduce the patient (name and age).
                 • Clearly state the main presenting issue/reason for referral/discharge of the patient
                    (e.g., who was recently diagnosed with cancer colon, etc.).
                 • Clearly state what action you are requesting from the recipient (e.g., for your kind
                    assessment, etc.).




                                                                                                                1

OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


            •   Body Paragraphs:
                 • Organize relevant information chronologically or by theme (e.g., medical history,
                   current presentation, investigations, treatment, progress, discharge plan). Inside each
                   paragraph, organize case notes logically.
                 • Use discourse markers (sometimes called "linking words" or "transition phrases")
                   appropriately.
                 • Group related information together in the same sentence, and use different sentence
                   types (simple, compound, and passive).
                 • Formulate case notes in your own words.
                 • Prioritize the most important information relevant to the purpose of the letter.
                 • Prioritize the most recent relevant information.
                 • Leave a blank line between paragraphs.
                 • Use indentation at the beginning of each paragraph.

            •   Conclusion/Request paragraph:
                 • Summarize the current situation.
                 • Clearly state what action you are requesting from the recipient (e.g., "I would be
                   grateful if you could take over Mr. Smith's ongoing care and monitor his blood
                   pressure." or "I would appreciate it if you could continue to review Ms. Jones's wound
                   and manage her pain as required.").
                 • Offer further information if needed (e.g., "Please do not hesitate to contact me if you
                   require any further information.").

            •   Closing: (e.g., Yours sincerely,)
            •   Your Title/Profession: (e.g., Nurse, Doctor, Physiotherapist etc.)

  3. Language and Tone:
      • Formal and Professional: Maintain a consistently formal and polite tone. Avoid slang,
        contractions (e.g., "don't," "can't"), and overly informal language.
      • Objective and Factual: Present facts and observations. Avoid personal judgments or emotional
        language.
      • Clear and Concise: Use clear, straightforward sentences. Avoid overly long or complex
        sentences. Get straight to the point.
      • Medical Terminology: Use appropriate medical terminology, but ensure it's understandable
        for the specific recipient. If writing to a non-medical professional (e.g., a community nurse in
        some contexts, or a social worker), explain complex terms briefly.
      • Accuracy: Ensure all medical facts, dates, medications, dosages, and patient details are
        accurate as per the case notes.
      • Grammar, Spelling, and Punctuation: These are crucial. Errors can affect clarity and your score.
        Proofread carefully.
      • Avoid "Suffers from": It's generally preferred to say "Mr. X has hypertension" instead of "Mr.
        X suffers from hypertension."




                                                                                                             2

OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


   4. Conciseness and Clarity:
       • Word Count: Aim for the suggested word count (usually 180-200 words for the body of the
         letter, excluding address, date, salutation, etc.). While not a strict penalty for slightly exceeding,
         it encourages conciseness.
       • Combine Details and avoid redundancy:
          1. Reorganize the selected relevant case notes.
          2. Merge connected case notes into one sentence.
          3. Don't repeat information unnecessarily.

   5. Time Management:
       • You have 45 minutes for the writing sub-test.
       • 5 minutes: Reading and planning.
       • 30-35 minutes: Writing the letter.
       • 5 minutes: Proofreading and editing.

   6. Paragraphing: In the OET Writing sub-test, you have two choices for paragraphing. While both are
        technically acceptable, one is much safer and clearer for the examiner.

         A. Block Style (Highly Recommended)
            This is the modern standard for medical and business correspondence.
              • How to do it: Start every line flush against the left-hand margin.
              • Paragraph separation: Leave one empty line between paragraphs.
              • Why use it: It is the cleanest look and makes it very easy for the examiner to see your
                 structure at a glance.

         B. Indented Style
            This is an older, more traditional format.
              • How to do it: The first line of each paragraph is moved in by about 5–7 spaces. You do
                 not necessarily need to leave a blank line between paragraphs if you indent.
              • Why avoid it: It can look messy if your indentations aren't uniform, and it is easier to
                 accidentally miss a paragraph break.

Specific Tips for Referral Letters
    •   Purpose: To explain why the patient needs to be seen by another healthcare professional and what
        specific input is required.

    •   Introduction: Clearly state you are referring the patient, their name, age, and the primary reason
        for referral.

    •   Body:
         • Provide relevant medical history leading up to the current presentation.
         • Detail the patient's current symptoms, findings, and any investigations performed.
         • Explain any treatment initiated and the patient's response.
         • Include relevant social history if it impacts the referral




                                                                                                                  3

OET Writing by Dr Amr Akmal


   •   Request: Be specific about what you are asking the recipient to do (e.g., "I would appreciate your
       urgent assessment regarding suitable pain management," or "I am referring Ms. Lee for a
       comprehensive neurological evaluation.").

   •   Referral Letter Opening Sentences: The key is to state clearly that you are referring the patient
       and the reason for the referral.
        • "I am writing to refer Mr. John Smith, a 67-year-old patient, for your urgent assessment
          regarding his worsening cardiac symptoms."
        • "Ms. Emily White, born on 12/03/1978, is being referred to you for further investigation and
          management of her persistent headaches."
        • "Thank you for seeing Mr. David Lee, a 45-year-old male, who presents with symptoms
          indicative of a possible deep vein thrombosis, requiring your urgent evaluation."
        • "I am referring Mrs. Sarah Green, aged 72, into your care for ongoing monitoring of her
          uncontrolled hypertension."
        • In conditions that don’t require referral, we use:
           a. I’m writing this letter to request/requesting your kind assessment of the workplace of Mr
              Jone, a 44-year-old patient of mine, who has clinical features suggestive of lumbar disc
              prolapse.
            b. I’m writing this letter in regard to/ regarding Mr Jone, a 44-year-old patient of mine, who
               has clinical features (or whose clinical features are) suggestive of/consistent with lumbar
               disc prolapse. Your assessment of his workplace would be highly appreciated.

   •   Referral Letter Finish Line:
        a. Simple Request for Assessment/Opinion
            • In view of the above, I believe that Mr John has features consistent with (or my provisional
              diagnosis is) lumbar disc prolapse.
            • "I would be grateful for your assessment and management of Mr. Henderson's persistent
              headaches."
            • "Your expert opinion on Ms. Davies' recurrent abdominal pain would be greatly
              appreciated."
            • "Thank you for seeing this patient and providing your recommendations regarding her
              ongoing care."
            • "I would appreciate your urgent review of Mrs. Chen's worsening cardiac symptoms."
            • "I would appreciate ordering a MRI scan for Mrs. Chen's and counseling her about the
              possibility of surgical intervention."

        b. Request for Specific Action/Intervention
            • "I would be grateful if you could assess Mr. Singh for potential surgical intervention for his
              fractured tibia."
            • "Please assess Mr. White for a comprehensive neurological evaluation and ongoing
              management."
            • "Your consideration of Ms. Tan for a gastric bypass procedure would be much appreciated."

OET Assessment Criteria:
The OET Writing sub-test is assessed on six criteria:
    1. Purpose (0-3 points):
        • Is the purpose of the letter immediately apparent?
        • Is the purpose sufficiently expanded throughout the letter? (i.e., does the content support the
          stated purpose?)

    2. Content (0-7 points):
        • Is all relevant information from the case notes included?
        • Is irrelevant information excluded?
        • Is the information accurate as per the case notes?

    3. Conciseness & Clarity (0-7 points):
        • Is the letter free from unnecessary details?
        • Is the information presented in clear language?
        • Are sentences well-structured and easy to understand?

    4. Genre & Style (0-7 points):
        • Is the letter appropriate for the audience and purpose (formal, professional, objective)?
        • Is the tone appropriate?
        • Are conventions of letter writing followed?

    5. Organization & Layout (0-7 points):
        • Is the information logically organized into paragraphs?
        • Is the layout of the letter correct (address, date, salutation, etc.)?
        • Are linking words and phrases used effectively to ensure coherence?

    6. Language (0-7 points):
        • Accuracy of grammar, spelling, and punctuation.
        • Appropriate use of vocabulary, including medical terminology.
        • Range of grammatical structures.


Using Time phrases:
    1. To Refer to Past Events (Medical History, Admission, Initial Presentation): These phrases are often
       used with the past simple or present perfect tense.
        • On admission/Upon admission: Used to describe events or findings when the patient was first
           admitted to the hospital.
            • Example: "On admission, Mr. Jones presented with severe abdominal pain."
            • Example: "Upon admission, his vital signs were stable."

         •   Initially: Refers to the beginning of a period or condition.
              • Example: "Initially, Ms. Lee responded well to the intravenous antibiotics."
              • Example: "Her symptoms initially resolved with rest."

        •   Previously/Prior to: Refers to events that happened before a specific point in time (e.g., before
            admission, before an operation).
             • Example: "Previously, Mr. Smith had no known allergies."
             • Example: "Prior to her surgery, Mrs. White experienced chronic knee pain."

        •   Subsequently: Refers to something that happened after something else.
             • Example: "He was subsequently diagnosed with Type 2 Diabetes."
             • Example: "Subsequently, his condition improved significantly."

        •   A week ago/Two days prior / Last [day/month]: Specific time markers for past events.
             • Example: "He reported a fall at home two days prior to admission."
             • Example: "Last Tuesday, she underwent a CT scan."

        •   In [month/year]/On [date]: For specific dates of past events.
             • Example: "In January 2024, she had a cholecystectomy."
             • Example: "On 15th May, he presented with a sudden onset of chest pain."

        •   Following [an event/procedure]: Used to describe what happened after a specific event or
            medical procedure.
             • Example: "Following the operation, he experienced some post-operative nausea."
             • Example: "Following his discharge, he will require daily wound dressings."

        •   Since then/Since [date]: To indicate a continuous period from a past point to the present.
             • Example: "He has been managing his diabetes well since then."
             • Example: "Since her admission on [date], her pain has significantly reduced."

        •   During hospitalization: Used to describe what happened after admission to hospital
             • Example: "During hospitalization, he experienced some nausea."
             • Example: " During hospitalization, he required daily assessment."

   2. To Refer to Ongoing/Current Events: These phrases often use the present continuous or present
      simple tense.
       • Currently: Refers to the present time.
          • Example: "Currently, Mr. Davies is mobilizing independently with a walking frame."
          • Example: "She is currently taking two medications daily."

        •   At present: Similar to currently.
             • Example: "At present, the patient's blood pressure is stable."

        •   Ongoing: To describe something that is continuing.
             • Example: "She requires ongoing physiotherapy."
             • Example: "His pain management is ongoing."

        •   Since [date of admission/beginning of treatment]: If referring to a condition or progress that
            started in the past and continues to the present.

            • Example: "Upon discharge, Mr. Patel will require supervision with his medication."

    1. Indefinite Articles: 'A' and 'An': These are used when you are referring to a singular, countable
       noun for the first time, or when you are talking about something in a general sense, not a specific

        • Mr. Jones presented with a persistent cough.
        • She reported a throbbing headache that began this morning.
        • Mrs. Chen developed a low-grade fever last night.

        • He is a smoker.
        • He has a history of hypertension. (Note: The phrase 'a history of' is countable, even though

        • She reported an ache in her left knee.
        • She reported pain in her left knee.

Discourse Markers in Professional Writing:
   1. Addition and Emphasis (To add related information or detail)
       • The patient's blood pressure remains elevated. In addition, his recent lipid panel showed
         hypercholesterolemia.
       • The wound shows signs of local infection. Furthermore, the patient's temperature has
         increased from 37.5°C to 38.9°C.
       • The initial blood tests confirmed an electrolyte imbalance. Moreover, the renal function
         markers showed acute deterioration.
       • The family reports previous episodes of unexplained syncope. Additionally, the patient has a
         known allergy to Penicillin.

       • The patient's pain score decreased initially with Tramadol. However, he now reports
         breakthrough pain every four hours.

         clinical presentation, we initiated empirical antibiotic therapy.
       • Surgical intervention carries a risk of nerve damage. On the other hand, delaying the
         procedure may lead to permanent loss of mobility.

         shows a significant reduction in CRP levels.

Identifying relevant vs irrelevant notes:
The Golden Rule: The Recipient and the Purpose
Always ask yourself these two questions:
  1. Who is the recipient? (e.g., GP, specialist, community nurse, physiotherapist, social worker). Will
     this case note affects how the recipient will continue care for the referred patient? or does the
     recipient need to know this case note to properly continue care for the referred patient?
 2. What is the purpose of the letter? (e.g., referral for specialist opinion, discharge for ongoing care,
    transfer to another facility, advice to a community service). Is this case note relevant to the purpose
    of the letter?

      The answers to these questions will dictate what information is relevant. Information is relevant if
the recipient needs it to effectively carry out their role in the patient's ongoing care based on the stated
purpose.
